lines: We have put a new boiler in and the old stack draws far too hard for it, and the
top of her is going anyway — there is a course near the cap you can pull out by
hand. We want twelve metres off her and a new cap on what is left.
She is good brick and we have a buyer for it, so we will pay you by what comes out
whole. Anything you break is ours to cart away and yours to explain.

bands.note: Nothing wrong with her down here and nothing is being asked of her either. This is the part you only have to climb.

Somebody laddered her before, and left his dogs in. They are forty years old and they look it. Whether a rusted dog is a gift or a trap is the first real decision of the day, and you find out by sounding it.
Where she will finish. Everything above this line is coming off; this course is the one the new cap sits on, so it is the one you must not damage.

Sixty years of flue gas and frost. Two joints in five will still take a dog and the rest will not, so this is the part of her you sound before you trust — it is the same skill as the survey and here it decides whether you get home.

The course the mill manager says you can pull out by hand. He is very nearly right, and that is the problem: one joint in four up here is worth a dog and you have to find it. Nothing you seat without sounding it first is going to hold you.

mission.flueCapacityNote: She is not connected to anything any more, so the bricks go down the flue and get barrowed out of the base. When it packs, it packs.
